personas.summary: Not-go as it stands, but only just: this is the most chemically clean chapter I have reviewed in this series, and the two things wrong with it are single clauses. I machine-verified every structure in the package with RDKit — all 32 asset SMILES and all 42 distinct SMILES appearing inside questions parse, and every stereodescriptor matches what the title, alt text and prose claim. The L/D audit is fully clean: the eighteen chiral L-amino acids drawn are (S), L-cysteine is (R), L-threonine is (2S,3R), L-isoleucine is (2S,3S), and both halves of the cystine disulfide are (R) — no D residue has crept in anywhere, which is the failure mode this package type is prone to. Every net formal charge matches its label (glycine +1/0/-1, alanine zwitterion 0, aspartate dianion -2, lysine dication +2). Every pI in the chapter recomputes correctly from the pKa values it states (Ala 6.02, Asp 2.95, His 7.59, Lys 9.74, Arg ~10.8), the Henderson-Hasselbalch worked example is right to two figures, 10^11 really is 15 kcal/mol of barrier, 0.99^100 really is 37 percent, and every one of the 40 answer keys is chemically correct — I re-derived all of them, including the Fischer configurations, the bond-change ledgers and the chymotrypsin mechanism selection. The claims about all six PDB entries check out against RCSB (1ZNI assembly 1 really is the A+B heterodimer the alt text describes; 1HHO assembly 1 really is the alpha-2 beta-2 tetramer). The blockers are (a) a sentence in the L-alanine figure description that asserts the (S) result for 'every L-amino acid whose side chain begins with carbon', which is exactly the claim the next figure exists to refute, and (b) an Edman walkthrough step that adds the amine across the wrong double bond of phenyl isothiocyanate, contradicting the next step of the same walkthrough. Beyond those, the real work is assessment alignment — the chapter's own flagship result (cysteine is R) and its own self-declared 'single most common error' (Strecker carbon bookkeeping) are never assessed — plus two sections that reason from a picture the student is never shown: the titration curve behind the pI section and the energy profile behind the enzyme section.

location.anchor_text: This is the configuration of every L-amino acid whose side chain begins with carbon.

findings.observation: The long_description of the L-alanine figure ends by generalising the (S) result to 'every L-amino acid whose side chain begins with carbon'. That is false. L-cysteine's side chain is CH2SH — it begins with carbon — and L-cysteine is (R). The sentence states, as a rule with no exception, precisely the rule whose exception the chapter's second section exists to teach.
findings.learner_impact: This figure appears in section 1 AND is repeated in section 2, the stereochemistry section, where it sits two figures above mol-l-cysteine. A student reading the figure descriptions in order is told a general rule and then shown a counterexample with no acknowledgement that the earlier statement was wrong; the most likely repair a student makes is to decide cysteine is somehow not an L-amino acid, or that the descriptor depends on something other than CIP priority. It also undercuts the section's genuinely excellent point that R/S is a labelling rule, not a shape.
findings.evidence: RDKit rdCIPLabeler on the package's own SMILES: mol-l-alanine 'N[C@@H](C)C(=O)O' -> C3H7NO2, CIP (1,'S'); mol-l-cysteine 'N[C@@H](CS)C(=O)O' -> C3H7NO2S, CIP (1,'R'). Both structures are correct; only the generalising sentence is wrong. The chapter prose itself states the correct version: 'Eighteen of the nineteen chiral standard amino acids are (S) in their L form.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The general claim attached to the L-alanine figure needs the cysteine exception carried with it, or needs to stop being a general claim at all. Nothing about the structures has to change.

location.anchor_text: Add the amine nitrogen across the carbon–sulfur double bond of the reagent.

findings.observation: Step 2 of the Edman walkthrough instructs the student to add the N-terminal amine across the C=S bond of phenyl isothiocyanate. The addition is across the C=N bond. The amine attacks the central carbon of Ph-N=C=S and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by re-forming C=S, giving the phenylthiocarbamoyl (thiourea) product Ph-NH-C(=S)-NH-peptide. The C=S survives; it is the C=N that is consumed. This is not a subtlety the step can be read past, because the whole point of the next cycle step is that the sulfur is still a thiocarbonyl sulfur and is therefore available to attack the first backbone carbonyl.
findings.learner_impact: A student who follows step 2 as written draws Ph-N=C(-SH)-NH-peptide and then cannot make step 4 work — the sulfur they need as the intramolecular nucleophile has become a thiol on a C=N, and the five-membered cyclisation no longer reads as the same reaction. Because the walkthrough is a stepwise scaffold, the student has no way to recover: the error is in the instruction, not in their work.
findings.evidence: Step 2 says 'Add the amine nitrogen across the carbon–sulfur double bond of the reagent.' Step 3 of the same walkthrough then correctly describes the product as one 'in which the sulfur-bearing carbon now carries the phenyl-substituted nitrogen from the reagent on one side and the N-terminal residue's nitrogen on the other' — i.e. a C=S flanked by two nitrogens, which can only arise from addition across C=N. The chapter's own expanded prose is also correct: 'attacks the electrophilic central carbon of the isothiocyanate to give a phenylthiocarbamoyl derivative.' The step is internally contradicted.
findings.recommended_outcome: Step 2 needs to name the bond that is actually consumed, consistent with step 3 and with the section prose. The rest of the walkthrough is correct and does not need touching.

location.anchor_text: glycine's alpha-ammonium ion comes in near 9.60

findings.observation: Glycine's alpha-ammonium pKa is given three different ways in student-facing content. The prose uses 9.60 and runs a full Henderson-Hasselbalch calculation on it (7.40 - 9.60 = -2.20, 0.63 percent free amine). The matching question states 2.35 and 9.78 with pI 6.06. The zwitterion and anion figure descriptions say the zwitterion dominates 'between roughly pH 2.3 and pH 9.8' and the anion 'above about pH 9.8'. The video brief also uses 2.35/9.78/6.06. Separately, the chapter states the alpha-COOH range as '2.0 to 2.4' and the alpha-ammonium range as '9.0 to 9.8', then supplies its own histidine alpha-COOH of 1.82 and aspartic acid alpha-NH3+ of 9.90, both outside those ranges.
findings.learner_impact: The pI section teaches students to compute, not to look up. A student who works glycine's pI from the reader's numbers gets 5.97; the assessment expects 6.06 and its distractor logic is built on 9.78. Worse, the H-H worked example — the one calculation the chapter asks students to reproduce — cannot be repeated with the pKa the question hands them. Students who notice will assume they have made an arithmetic error; students who do not will carry two incompatible sets of numbers into an exam.
findings.evidence: nugget-zwitterions-and-acid-base-behaviour: 'Methylammonium ion has a pKa of 10.6, whereas glycine's alpha-ammonium ion comes in near 9.60'; 'log([NH2]/[NH3+]) = 7.40 − 9.60 = −2.20 ... about 0.63 percent' (I recompute 10^-2.20 = 6.31e-3, fraction 0.627% — correct for 9.60). ch26-match-glycine-ph-species prompt: 'pKa values of 2.35 for its COOH group and 9.78 for its NH3+ group, and an isoelectric point of 6.06' ((2.35+9.78)/2 = 6.065 — self-consistent, but not consistent with 9.60, which gives 5.97). mol-glycine-zwitterion long_description: 'between roughly pH 2.3 and pH 9.8'. video-zwitterion-titration narration_outline: '2.35 for the carboxyl and 9.78 for the ammonium ... 6.06'.
findings.recommended_outcome: One glycine pKa pair has to be authoritative across prose, figure descriptions, the question and the video brief, and the two stated pKa ranges need to actually contain the chapter's own histidine and aspartic acid values.

location.anchor_text: Nineteen are S, cysteine is R, and nothing moved

findings.observation: The stereochemistry concept carries three learning objectives, the second of which is 'Assign R or S at the alpha carbon of a given amino acid using CIP priorities, and account for cysteine being (R) while the other eighteen chiral L-amino acids are (S)'. It is assessed by exactly two questions, both of them Fischer-projection builds (ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer and its threonine variant). Neither asks for a CIP assignment, neither involves cysteine, and nothing anywhere in the 40-question bank tests the cysteine exception, the priority swap that causes it, or the fact that no atom moves. This is the section the chapter titles after and spends its best writing on.
findings.learner_impact: The single most examinable and most misremembered fact in the chapter is taught and then never retrieved. Students reliably forget which residue is the exception and why; without a retrieval opportunity they will encode 'L equals S' and be wrong on cysteine, and they will also miss the transferable idea that a descriptor can flip without a bond changing. The Fischer questions that do exist test the D/L convention, which is a different objective (LO 1).
findings.evidence: Question bank by concept: amino-acid-stereochemistry has 2 of 40 questions, both question_type 'fischer' (ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer, ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer-v2). Grepping all 40 prompt_texts and answer_keys for cysteine: it appears only as a rank_order card in ch26-rank-isoelectric-points-v2, where it is used for its thiol pKa (8.3) in a pI calculation, not for its configuration.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs at least one retrieval opportunity on the CIP assignment at the alpha carbon and on why cysteine's descriptor differs while its spatial arrangement does not.

location.anchor_text: Start from the titration curve, because reading it backwards is how the whole idea is built.

findings.observation: The isoelectric point section is constructed entirely around a titration curve — it opens by telling the student to read one backwards, describes its shape plateau by plateau, tells them that counting plateaus counts ionizable groups, locates the zwitterion in the steep region between plateaus and the pI within that region, and then generalises to three-plateau curves. No such curve exists anywhere in the chapter. The section's seven figures are all flat 2D structures of individual species, and the chapter as a whole compiles 53 molecule blocks, 8 images and zero plot-type blocks.
findings.learner_impact: Every claim in the section that carries real conceptual weight — plateau equals buffer region, midpoint equals pKa, count plateaus to count groups, the flanking pair is the pair bracketing the flat neutral region — is a claim about a graph the student cannot see. Students who already know what a titration curve looks like will follow; the ones the section is written for will read a page of geometric description with nothing to anchor it and will fall back on memorising 'average the two lowest for acidic, two highest for basic'. That is exactly the rote outcome the section says it wants to prevent.
findings.evidence: nugget-isoelectric-point asset_ids: mol-l-alanine-zwitterion, mol-l-aspartic-acid, mol-l-aspartate-dianion, mol-l-lysine, mol-l-lysine-dication, mol-l-histidine, mol-l-glutamic-acid — all molecule type. Compiled reader section 'nugget-isoelectric-point' contains 1 text block, 7 molecule blocks, 1 external_link block. Prose: 'a flat buffering plateau centred near pH 2.34, a steep climb, a second flat plateau centred near pH 9.69, and a final steep climb ... A titration curve is therefore a direct readout of a molecule's pKa values, and counting plateaus counts ionizable groups.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The pI section needs the titration curve it reasons from to be visible and readable — with the plateaus, the two pKa midpoints, the steep neutral region and the pI marked — for at least the neutral-side-chain case and one three-ionization case.

location.anchor_text: A catalyst lowers ΔG‡ and leaves ΔG° alone.

findings.observation: The enzyme section's central claim is a statement about two different vertical distances on an energy profile: the catalyst lowers the barrier and does not move the endpoints, so both rate constants rise by the same factor and K is untouched. It is asserted three times in prose, it is the discriminator in the keyed multi_select question, and the transition-state-stabilisation argument depends on distinguishing where binding energy is paid out along that same coordinate. The chapter has no energy diagram of any kind. Peer reader chapters in this series carry reaction_coordinate blocks for exactly this purpose; this chapter compiles zero.
findings.learner_impact: The ΔG‡ versus ΔG° confusion is the single most persistent misconception in this topic, and it is a spatial confusion — students merge the barrier height with the reaction free energy because they are holding one undifferentiated mental picture. Asserting the distinction in words three times does not separate them. The transition-state-stabilisation point suffers the same way: 'binding interactions only partly formed in the ES complex are fully realised at the transition state' is a statement about which point on a curve gets lowered, and students who cannot see the curve will read it as 'the enzyme binds the substrate tightly', which the text explicitly warns against.
findings.evidence: nugget-enzymes-and-catalysis asset_ids: pdb-lysozyme-fold, pdb-citrate-synthase, mol-l-cysteine, mol-l-lysine, mol-l-glutamine — no energy-profile asset. Compiled reader block census for this chapter: {'text': 10, 'molecule': 53, 'mcmurry_link': 1, 'external_link': 10, 'image': 8}; no 'reaction_coordinate' blocks, whereas e.g. alkenes-structure-and-reactivity.json carries 4 and biomolecules-carbohydrates.json carries 1. Keyed question ch26-enzyme-catalysis-select distinguishes option a (ΔG‡ smaller: correct) from option b (ΔG° smaller: incorrect) and option c (K unchanged: correct).
findings.recommended_outcome: The enzyme section needs the catalysed and uncatalysed profiles shown on one coordinate so that the lowered barrier and the unchanged endpoints are separately visible, and so the transition-state-stabilisation argument has a place to point.

location.anchor_text: The polar uncharged family — serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine, and glutamine

findings.observation: The prose teaches a five-family scheme (nonpolar aliphatic, aromatic, polar uncharged, acidic, basic) and names the polar uncharged family exhaustively as serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine and glutamine, with tyrosine explicitly assigned to the aromatic family. The assessment then uses a four-bin scheme with no aromatic bin (ch26-sort-side-chain-classes offers only nonpolar / polar-neutral / acidic / basic), and ch26-select-polar-neutral-side-chains keys L-tyrosine as a correct selection for 'polar but carries no net charge at pH 7'.
findings.learner_impact: A student who learned the chapter's own five-family table selects serine and glutamine, omits tyrosine, and is marked wrong on a question whose feedback then tells them tyrosine 'belongs in the selection'. The learning objective they were given says to sort side chains into one of five families 'using the behaviour of the side chain in water'; the assessment silently switches to a property test on a four-bin taxonomy. Both taxonomies are defensible in isolation; running them in the same chapter without saying so is what causes the damage.
findings.evidence: nugget-amino-acid-structure-and-classification: 'The aromatic family is phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan'; 'The polar uncharged family — serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine, and glutamine'. ch26-select-polar-neutral-side-chains answer_key correct_option_ids [redacted] where f = L-Tyrosine. ch26-sort-side-chain-classes groups: g1 'Nonpolar (hydrophobic)', g2 'Polar, neutral at pH 7', g3 'Acidic', g4 'Basic' — no aromatic group, and no aromatic residue among the eight items.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs one taxonomy that prose and assessment both use, or an explicit statement that the aromatic family cross-cuts the polar/nonpolar test and where tyrosine lands under each.

location.anchor_text: Trypsin hydrolyses peptide bonds on the carboxyl side of the basic residues lysine and arginine

findings.observation: The protease specificities are stated as exceptionless rules. Trypsin does not cleave Lys-Pro or Arg-Pro bonds, and chymotrypsin likewise skips Xaa-Pro; cyanogen bromide also fails at Met-Pro and converts the methionine to a homoserine lactone rather than leaving it intact. None of this is mentioned. The chapter has just spent a whole section establishing that proline's ring nitrogen makes it behave differently from every other residue, so the exception is both important and already motivated.
findings.learner_impact: The overlapping-fragment logic the section teaches depends on predicting where a protease cuts. A student who applies 'trypsin cuts after every K and R' to a sequence containing K-P will predict fragments that do not exist and will conclude their overlap reconstruction is wrong. This is a standard exam scenario, and it is also the place where the chapter's own proline material would pay off a second time.
findings.evidence: nugget-peptide-sequencing expanded tier: 'Trypsin hydrolyses peptide bonds on the carboxyl side of the basic residues lysine and arginine; chymotrypsin cleaves after the bulky aromatic residues phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan; cyanogen bromide cleaves after methionine.' No proline qualifier appears in any tier. Contrast the same chapter's careful treatment at nugget-peptide-bond-structure: 'Proline breaks this pattern, and it breaks it for a structural reason worth stating carefully.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The cleavage-specificity rules need their proline exception attached, ideally tied back to the structural reason the chapter has already established.

location.anchor_text: Its practical ceiling is about fifty residues, and the reason is arithmetic rather than chemistry

findings.observation: The only limit given for the Edman degradation is the ~50-cycle ceiling from compounding inefficiency. The chapter does not mention that a blocked N-terminus defeats the method outright — N-terminal acetylation and N-terminal pyroglutamate are both common in real proteins and both leave nothing for phenyl isothiocyanate to react with, so the first cycle returns nothing at all and the chemist learns only that the terminus is blocked.
findings.learner_impact: The section's whole design principle is 'only the free alpha-amino group reacts' — it says so three times, and the walkthrough turns on it. The natural next question, which a good student will ask, is what happens when there is no free alpha-amino group; leaving it unanswered means students take a null Edman result as an experimental failure rather than as a positive structural finding. It is also a standard exam scenario paired with the tryptophan and Asn/Gln distortions the chapter does cover well.
findings.evidence: nugget-peptide-sequencing expanded tier lists exactly one limitation of Edman ('Its practical ceiling is about fifty residues'). The three hydrolysis limitations are, by contrast, treated thoroughly ('tryptophan does not survive ... the side-chain amides of asparagine and glutamine hydrolyse ... Serine and threonine suffer partial destruction'). Concept learning objective 2 for peptide-sequencing names only the fifty-cycle limit.
findings.recommended_outcome: The Edman section needs the blocked-N-terminus failure mode alongside the cycle-count ceiling, framed as diagnostic information rather than as failure.

location.anchor_text: Getting that carbon count wrong is the single most common error on Strecker problems.

findings.observation: The chapter identifies the Strecker carbon bookkeeping — that cyanide supplies the carboxyl carbon, so the aldehyde is one carbon shorter than students expect, and phenylalanine comes from phenylacetaldehyde rather than benzaldehyde — as 'the single most common error on Strecker problems', and repeats the point in the practice_check. No question in the bank tests it. The two synthesis_route questions cover amidomalonate alkylation and HVZ/ammonolysis; the Strecker short_answer variant supplies the aldehyde, the intermediate and the product in the prompt and asks only for the reaction's name.
findings.learner_impact: The chapter flags an error, explains it, and then gives students no chance to make it in a low-stakes setting where feedback can catch them. Naming a reaction whose full mechanism is spelled out in the prompt is recall of a word, not of the chemistry the section says matters; the objective 'choose the correct starting material for a target side chain in each of the four routes' goes unassessed for the one route where the choice is counterintuitive.
findings.evidence: nugget-amino-acid-synthesis expanded tier: 'alanine comes from acetaldehyde, not from pyruvic acid, and phenylalanine comes from phenylacetaldehyde, not from benzaldehyde. Getting that carbon count wrong is the single most common error on Strecker problems.' ch26-racemic-amino-acid-synthesis-v2 prompt gives 'Acetaldehyde is stirred with NH3 and HCN, giving an alpha-aminonitrile, CH3CH(NH2)C≡N ... alanine is obtained. Name this classical amino-acid synthesis.' answer_key answer_text [redacted] of 'Strecker'. Neither synthesis_route question uses the Strecker route.
findings.recommended_outcome: The synthesis section needs a retrieval opportunity in which the student picks the carbon source for a Strecker target, with benzaldehyde-for-phenylalanine available as the productive wrong turn.

location.anchor_text: Backbone N–H groups of the enzyme donate hydrogen bonds to the developing negative charge on the tetrahedral intermediate, stabilising it.

findings.observation: The chymotrypsin question keys option (d), the oxyanion hole, as a correct selection. The oxyanion hole is never mentioned in this chapter in any depth tier. The chapter's serine-protease coverage is one sentence under covalent catalysis ('A serine hydroxyl, activated by a neighbouring histidine and aspartate, attacks an amide carbonyl to give a covalent acyl-enzyme that is hydrolysed in a second stage'), and its two worked enzymes are lysozyme and citrate synthase, neither of which is assessed anywhere.
findings.learner_impact: In a multi_select, an unrecognised true statement is functionally indistinguishable from a distractor: a student who has learned the chapter well will leave (d) unselected on the reasonable ground that the chapter never said it, and will lose the item. The question is well built and the chemistry is right — it is simply testing a fact from outside the chapter. Meanwhile the two enzymes the chapter does develop in detail, with named residues and full mechanisms, are assessed by nothing at all.
findings.evidence: Searching all ten nuggets across all three depth tiers for 'oxyanion', 'tetrahedral intermediate' and 'backbone N–H ... intermediate' returns no match; the closest text is the covalent-catalysis paragraph in nugget-enzymes-and-catalysis. ch26-enzyme-catalysis-select-v2 answer_key correct_option_ids [redacted]. Neither ch26-enzyme-catalysis-select nor its v2 mentions lysozyme, Glu35, Asp52, citrate synthase, acetyl CoA or oxaloacetate.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the oxyanion hole needs to be taught in the covalent-catalysis paragraph where the serine proteases already appear, or the enzyme assessment needs to be built on the lysozyme and citrate synthase chemistry the chapter actually develops.

location.anchor_text: The peptide bond is an amide, and Chapter 21 already showed how to make an amide

findings.observation: Five bare chapter-number cross-references appear in the compiled reader prose — 'Chapter 21' and 'Chapter 11' twice in the peptide synthesis section, 'Chapter 25' and 'Chapter 23' in the enzymes section. These are McMurry numbers. The same package's textbook_matching maps this chapter to Klein chapter 25 and to McMurry Fundamentals chapter 23, which are the very numbers being used as pointers to other topics.
findings.learner_impact: A Klein student reading 'chemistry taken directly from Chapter 25' is pointed at the chapter they are currently reading; a Fundamentals student reading 'enolate chemistry from Chapter 23' is pointed at the same. The reader is explicitly textbook-agnostic and carries per-textbook mappings, so a number with no book attached resolves differently for different students in the same class. The references are also the chapter's main mechanism for connecting new material to prior learning, which is the thing they most need to do reliably.
findings.evidence: Compiled reader text blocks contain: 'Chapter 21 already showed how to make an amide'; 'one already met in Chapter 11 and Chapter 21'; 'chemistry taken directly from Chapter 25'; 'enolate chemistry from Chapter 23'. topic.package.json textbook_matching.overrides maps this package to mcmurry-organic-chemistry-6e ch 26, mcmurry-fundamentals-organic-chemistry-6e ch 23, klein-organic-chemistry-4e ch 25, openstax-organic-chemistry-current ch 26.
findings.recommended_outcome: Prior-topic references need to resolve for every mapped textbook — by naming the topic rather than a number, or by carrying the book with the number.

findings.observation: The peptide bond concept has six questions: two curved-arrow (resonance donation, hydroxide addition), two hotspot (locate the amide bond, locate the donating nitrogen) and two bond-change ledgers (condensation, hydrolysis). Every one of them is about connectivity or electron flow. Its second learning objective — identify the six coplanar atoms, state why trans dominates, and explain why proline is the exception — is not assessed by any of them, nor is the phi/psi point, nor the rotation barrier. Roughly half the section's prose is about geometry that no question touches.
findings.learner_impact: Peptide-unit planarity, trans dominance and the proline exception are the parts of this section that later sections depend on: the helix, the sheet, the Ramachandran argument, and the proline-in-a-helix reasoning in the protein-structure practice check all assume them. Students will have practised the electron-pushing account and not the geometric consequence, which is the part they are asked to use downstream.
findings.evidence: Question bank for concept peptide-bond-structure: ch26-amide-resonance-arrow(+v2), ch26-locate-peptide-bond(+v2), ch26-peptide-bond-ledger(+v2). None mentions cis, trans, planar, coplanar, phi, psi, Ramachandran or proline in prompt or answer key. Concept learning objective 2 reads 'Identify the six atoms that lie in the plane of one peptide unit, state why the trans arrangement of the two alpha carbons dominates, and explain why proline is the one residue for which the cis arrangement is competitive.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The peptide-bond section needs at least one retrieval opportunity on the geometric consequence — which atoms are coplanar, why trans wins, and why proline is the exception — rather than only on the electron flow that produces it.

location.anchor_text: a 100-residue chain is obtained in 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 37 percent

findings.observation: The peptide synthesis concept's third learning objective ends 'and calculate how a per-step yield compounds over a long sequence'. The chapter develops the arithmetic carefully and correctly (0.99^100 = 37 percent, 0.995^100 = 61 percent, and the observation that the missing material is a family of deletion sequences). No question in the bank asks for that calculation; the only two numeric_with_units questions are both pI computations.
findings.learner_impact: This is the argument that explains why solid-phase synthesis has a practical size limit and why long targets are made as fragments — it is the section's payoff and the one place a number carries the point. Reading a worked multiplication is not the same as performing one, and students consistently underestimate how fast a high per-step yield decays.
findings.evidence: Concept peptide-synthesis learning objective 3: 'Outline one cycle of Merrifield solid-phase synthesis, identify the by-product of a DCC coupling, and calculate how a per-step yield compounds over a long sequence.' Questions for this concept: ch26-boc-vs-fmoc-matrix(+v2), ch26-draw-boc-glycine(+v2) — protecting groups and the DCU by-product only. numeric_with_units questions in the bank: ch26-histidine-isoelectric-point (pI 7.59) and ch26-histidine-isoelectric-point-v2 (pI 2.95).
findings.recommended_outcome: The solid-phase section needs a retrieval opportunity on compounding yield, since that arithmetic is the stated objective and the section's concluding argument.

location.anchor_text: between a single bond at 1.47 and a double bond at 1.27, implying roughly forty percent double-bond character

findings.observation: The chapter presents the forty percent double-bond figure as following from the bond length. Interpolating linearly between the quoted endpoints gives (1.47 - 1.32)/(1.47 - 1.27) = 0.75, i.e. about seventy-five percent, not forty. The forty percent figure is a standard textbook number derived from resonance-structure weighting, not from bond length; the word 'implying' asserts an inference the numbers do not support.
findings.learner_impact: Students who do the subtraction — and the sentence invites them to, by supplying all three lengths — get a number nearly twice the one they are told follows from it, and have no way to tell which is wrong. It also models a bad habit: treating bond length as linearly proportional to bond order. Both individual facts are fine; only the causal link between them is not.
findings.evidence: nugget-peptide-bond-structure expanded tier: 'The amide C-N bond measures about 1.32 angstroms, between a single bond at 1.47 and a double bond at 1.27, implying roughly forty percent double-bond character.' Arithmetic: (1.47-1.32)/(1.47-1.27) = 0.15/0.20 = 0.75.
findings.recommended_outcome: The forty percent figure needs to stand on its own basis rather than be presented as a consequence of the bond lengths quoted beside it.

location.anchor_text: alanine comes from acetaldehyde, not from pyruvic acid

findings.observation: The Strecker carbon-bookkeeping point is made with two contrasts. The second is exactly right: phenylalanine comes from phenylacetaldehyde, not benzaldehyde, because benzaldehyde would give phenylglycine. The first is not parallel: pyruvic acid is not an aldehyde and is not a candidate Strecker substrate at all — it is the alpha-keto acid that gives alanine by reductive amination, which the same section teaches two paragraphs earlier.
findings.learner_impact: The contrast that is supposed to sharpen the Strecker carbon count instead blurs the boundary between two of the four routes. A student can reasonably read 'alanine comes from acetaldehyde, not from pyruvic acid' as ruling pyruvic acid out as an alanine precursor generally, which is false and undoes the reductive amination material.
findings.evidence: nugget-amino-acid-synthesis expanded tier: 'Because cyanide supplies the carboxyl carbon, the aldehyde must be one carbon shorter than you might first assume: alanine comes from acetaldehyde, not from pyruvic acid, and phenylalanine comes from phenylacetaldehyde, not from benzaldehyde.' Same section, earlier: 'glutamate dehydrogenase performs a genuine reductive amination on alpha-ketoglutarate' and 'If the alpha-keto acid is available, ammonia condenses with its ketone carbonyl to give an imine'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The Strecker carbon-count contrast needs a comparator that is a plausible aldehyde choice, so it does not collide with the reductive amination route taught in the same section.

location.anchor_text: Aspartate above pH 10: both carboxyls deprotonated

findings.observation: The figure title names 'both carboxyls deprotonated' as what characterises the species. Both carboxyls are already deprotonated in the -1 monoanion that dominates from about pH 4 to pH 9.9; what makes this the dianion is that the alpha-ammonium group has also lost its proton, leaving a neutral amine. The alt text and long_description both get this right; only the title points at the wrong feature.
findings.learner_impact: In the pI section the whole exercise is walking the charge down one ionization at a time and identifying which step produces which species. A title that identifies the dianion by a feature the previous species already had works directly against that discipline, and titles are what students skim.

location.anchor_text: Rotation is genuinely free about the two bonds on either side of that plate

findings.observation: The terse and standard tiers, and the practice_check answer, describe phi and psi rotation as 'free' or 'entirely free' without qualification, and then in the next breath invoke the Ramachandran plot. The Ramachandran plot exists precisely because those rotations are not free — most of phi/psi space is sterically forbidden, and the expanded tier says so ('subject only to steric clashes between neighbouring plates and side chains ... how little of that two-dimensional space is accessible'). The qualifier is present only in the tier the reader happens to compile.
findings.learner_impact: Students who use the terse or standard tier for revision, or who read the practice_check answer, get 'free rotation' and 'only these small regions are allowed' side by side with no reconciliation. The distinction that matters — free of an electronic barrier, but heavily constrained sterically — is the one that makes the alpha helix and beta sheet look inevitable rather than arbitrary.
findings.evidence: terse tier: 'Rotation remains free about N-Cα (phi) and Cα-C (psi), and those two angles are the backbone's only real freedom.' standard tier: 'Rotation is entirely free about the two bonds that flank each plate.' practice_check answer: 'Rotation is genuinely free about the two bonds on either side of that plate, N-Cα (the angle phi) and Cα-C (the angle psi).' expanded tier (the compiled reader tier) is correctly qualified.

strengths: Structural fidelity is the best I have seen in this chapter series. Every one of the 32 asset SMILES and all 42 distinct SMILES inside questions parse; every stereodescriptor matches its claim; and the specific traps this topic sets are all avoided — L-cysteine is (R), L-threonine is (2S,3R), L-isoleucine is (2S,3S), and both alpha carbons of the cystine disulfide are (R), so neither half has silently become D.

The ionisation-state figures are exactly right, which is unusual. RDKit confirms glycine cation +1 with COOH and NH3+, zwitterion 0 with both full charges present, anion -1 with neutral NH2, alanine zwitterion 0 with S retained, aspartate dianion -2 with a neutral amine, and lysine dication +2 with an intact COOH.

Every numeric claim I recomputed is correct: pI values 6.02 / 2.95 / 9.74 / 7.59 / ~10.8 all follow from the stated pKa pairs; the Henderson-Hasselbalch worked example gives 0.63 percent free amine and 1.1e5 carboxylate ratio as claimed; 10^11 rate enhancement really is 15.0 kcal/mol at 298 K; 0.99^100 = 37 percent and 0.995^100 = 61 percent.

All six PDB claims check out against RCSB. 1ZNI biological assembly 1 really is the A+B heterodimer the alt text describes rather than the Zn hexamer, and 1HHO assembly 1 really is the alpha-2 beta-2 tetramer — both are the kind of claim that usually fails silently.

All 40 answer keys are chemically correct on re-derivation, including the two Fischer builds (I verified 2S,3R corresponds to NH2 left at C2 and OH right at C3), both bond-change ledgers, the cysteine-below-alanine pI ordering that turns on the thiol pKa sitting between the alpha values, and the chymotrypsin selection.

The account of why all four classical syntheses give racemates is careful and correct route by route, including the subtle amidomalonate case — the alkylated carbon is not a stereocentre at all, and the centre is created only at the decarboxylation enol.

The peptide-bond treatment is unusually rigorous: it gets the trans arrangement's Z descriptor right, states the proline exception with its structural cause rather than as a rule, gives realistic cis populations, and names peptidyl-prolyl isomerases as the biological consequence.

The enzyme section states the catalyst boundary precisely and repeatedly — lowers ΔG‡, leaves ΔG° and K alone, raises both rate constants equally — and the lysozyme account goes as far as the covalent glycosyl-enzyme refinement and net retention, which most texts at this level skip.

The wrong-answer feedback is specific and diagnostic throughout rather than generic. The rank_order pI feedback in particular diagnoses the exact wrong ordering the student submitted and explains why cysteine's thiol pKa moves the bracketing pair.
Denaturation is handled with a nuance most chapters miss: it names the disulfides as usually surviving, rather than lumping all cross-links together as noncovalent.
open_questions: None of the ten authored practice_checks compiles into the reader — the reader carries only text, molecule, image and link blocks. I checked fifteen sibling chapters and none compiles practice blocks either, so I have treated this as a platform norm rather than a chapter defect. If it is not intended, this chapter is losing ten strong worked answers.

The reader compiles the expanded tier for all ten sections. Several of my tier-specific observations (instr-018) only bite if the terse or standard tiers are surfaced anywhere — in study-guide exports, deck notes or LMS packaging. Where are the non-expanded tiers actually shown to students?

5CSC is the OPEN form of chicken heart citrate synthase with no ligands deposited, but the figure's long_description says the substrates bind in a cavity 'which closes around them'. That is a correct statement about induced fit and a reasonable use of the entry, but a reader comparing the image to the caption sees an empty open cleft. Is the open form the deliberate choice?

The chapter has no question at all on the four classical syntheses' shared racemate limitation beyond a one-word short answer, and no question on lysozyme or citrate synthase. Was the enzyme and synthesis assessment scoped down deliberately, or is this chapter's bank still being built out?

personas.summary: The writing in this chapter is genuinely good at the sentence level - it names the wrong moves I would actually make ("L-Cysteine is (R)... and no atom has moved", "the structure most often drawn for an amino acid... is a convenient fiction"), it works the pI calculation four separate times, and the wrong-answer explanations on the questions teach the discriminating idea instead of just saying I was wrong. What defeats me is the chapter as delivered. The compiled reader gives me exactly one thing per section: the full expanded essay, 5,000-8,700 characters of unbroken prose, followed by a pile of flat 2D molecule pictures. The terse and standard tiers never reach me, all ten practice checks never reach me, all three video briefs never reach me, and there is not one checkpoint, summary, or key-points box anywhere in ten sections. Every figure in the chapter is a static structure or an RCSB ribbon photograph, so every spatial claim the chapter makes - the six coplanar atoms of the peptide unit, phi and psi, the Ramachandran plot, the i-to-i+4 helix hydrogen bond, 3.6 residues per turn, side chains alternating above and below a sheet, and above all the titration curve that section 4 says it is going to read backwards - is a sentence I have to take on faith and then get quizzed on. The two places I actually stop are the synthesis section, which recaps four different prior chapters' reactions in one sentence each, and the peptide-synthesis section, which states the rule "block every reactive group except the two that must react" and then never works a single case in front of me (the one worked case is in a practice check I never see). I can pass most of these twenty questions by pattern-matching the prose; I could not reconstruct the chapter's chemistry from what I was shown.

findings.observation: The prose teaches a five-family classification with 'aromatic' as its own family, and files tyrosine there while noting it 'sometimes appears in the acidic column of older tables'. The questions then use a different scheme. ch26-sort-side-chain-classes offers four groups (Nonpolar, Polar-neutral, Acidic, Basic) with no aromatic group at all, and ch26-select-polar-neutral-side-chains requires tyrosine to be selected as polar-uncharged, with the wrong-answer text saying 'It belongs in the selection'. The learning objective for this concept explicitly says 'one of the five families'.
findings.learner_impact: I memorised five families with tyrosine under aromatic. The first question I meet has four boxes and none of them is the one I put tyrosine in, so I now believe I learned the classification wrong. That is the point where I stop trusting my notes and start guessing.

findings.recommended_outcome: The classification scheme the student is taught and the classification scheme the student is graded on must be the same one, or the relationship between the two must be stated where the student meets the second.

location.anchor_text: Carries a strongly UV-absorbing aromatic ring system, so each deprotection can be followed by monitoring the effluent

findings.observation: The f_uv row of this matrix tests a fact the chapter never states. Neither the terse, standard, nor expanded tier of nugget-peptide-synthesis mentions ultraviolet absorption, effluent monitoring, or any analytical use of the fluorene ring; searching the whole chapter for 'UV', 'ultraviolet', or 'absorb' returns only the amide IR remark and the tryptophan 280 nm point in a different section. Hint 3 points me at 'a fused tricyclic aromatic system' but never links that to UV absorbance, so I still have to import the connection from elsewhere.
findings.learner_impact: Two of the ten cells in this matrix are unanswerable from the chapter, so I lose them, and because they are the only rows I could not reason out I read the whole matrix as evidence that I did not study properly.

findings.recommended_outcome: Either the chapter should teach why the Fmoc chromophore is analytically useful, or this row should not be graded.

location.anchor_text: Draw the energy profile of a reaction and mark three things on it: the starting level, the finishing level, and the height of the hump between them.

findings.observation: The final section is marked depth 'advanced', 9 minutes, and 8,699 characters, and in that span introduces deltaG-double-dagger versus deltaG-degrees, energetic coupling to ATP, the six enzyme classes, active site, induced fit, four separate sources of rate enhancement, transition-state analogues, catalytic antibodies, active-site pKa tuning, serine and cysteine proteases, aldolase enamine chemistry, the full lysozyme mechanism (oxocarbenium character, covalent glycosyl-enzyme intermediate, retention of configuration), the citrate synthase aldol, metal cofactors, five named coenzymes, and apo/holoenzyme. Its five figures are two ribbon photographs and three unrelated amino-acid structures (cysteine, lysine, glutamine). There is no energy diagram anywhere in the chapter - yet the first hint of the section's only question instructs me to draw one.
findings.learner_impact: The chapter's densest section is also its least supported, and it arrives when I am most tired. I skim it, and when the question's first hint tells me to draw the energy profile, I realise the chapter never showed me one and I answer the whole multi-select from wording rather than from a picture of the barrier.
findings.evidence: nuggets[nugget-enzymes-and-catalysis]: depth 'advanced', duration_minutes 9, expanded length 8,699 chars, asset_ids ['pdb-lysozyme-fold','pdb-citrate-synthase','mol-l-cysteine','mol-l-lysine','mol-l-glutamine']. ch26-enzyme-catalysis-select hints[0]: 'Draw the energy profile of a reaction and mark three things on it'. Package asset type census contains no reaction_coordinate or energy-diagram asset.
findings.recommended_outcome: The load in this section needs to be broken up, and the barrier-versus-endpoints distinction - which is the section's single most important idea and the thing the question hint depends on - needs a representation the student can actually look at.

location.anchor_text: L-cysteine is (R) while the other eighteen chiral L-amino acids are (S) - and no atom has moved.

findings.observation: The stereochemistry section carries three learning objectives - the meaning of L, assigning R/S and accounting for cysteine, and identifying threonine and isoleucine as (2S,3R) and (2S,3S) - and the only surfaced question on this concept is ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer, which exercises the first objective alone. The cysteine descriptor flip, presented as the section's headline result and reinforced in the section title itself, is never assessed by any of the twenty questions; neither are threonine and isoleucine, whose structures are provided as figures. The zwitterion concept has the parallel problem: its third objective is 'Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship with real pKa values to calculate the ratio', and no surfaced question requires a Henderson-Hasselbalch calculation (the only numeric question is a pI average).
findings.learner_impact: The one idea I was most worried I did not understand is the one I am never asked about, so I never find out whether I understand it. I would have used a question here to calibrate; instead I go into an exam with an untested belief about the hardest point in the chapter.
findings.evidence: Surfaced questions by concept: amino-acid-stereochemistry = 1 (ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer, a Fischer projection placement task); zwitterions-and-acid-base-behaviour = 1 (ch26-match-glycine-ph-species, a pH-to-species matching task). Section title: 'Nineteen are S, cysteine is R, and nothing moved'.
findings.recommended_outcome: Each concept's headline objective needs at least one place where the student produces the answer; two core concepts currently have objectives with no corresponding practice.

location.anchor_text: the amino group occupies the same horizontal position - the one the hydroxyl occupies in L-glyceraldehyde.

findings.observation: The final hint of this question - the last help available before I am wrong - defers to L-glyceraldehyde rather than resolving the question. L-glyceraldehyde appears exactly once in the entire chapter ('The reference compound is L-glyceraldehyde by way of L-serine'), it is never drawn, and its configuration is never stated. So hint 3 tells me the answer is 'wherever the hydroxyl is in a molecule the chapter never shows me'. The rule I actually need - amino group on the left - is stated only in the generic_incorrect_explanation, which I see only after I have already answered wrong.
findings.learner_impact: I exhaust the hint ladder and still cannot place the group, so I pick a side at random. The rule arrives as a consolation prize after I have been marked wrong, which is the sequence that makes me feel the material is not learnable.
findings.evidence: ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer hints[2].text; generic_incorrect_explanation: 'the amino group goes on the left for an L-amino acid and on the right for a D-amino acid'. nugget-amino-acid-stereochemistry expanded: 'The reference compound is L-glyceraldehyde by way of L-serine' - the only occurrence, with no figure.
findings.recommended_outcome: The last hint in a ladder must be usable on its own; here it depends on a reference compound the chapter neither draws nor describes.

location.anchor_text: an E1cb elimination then expels dibenzofulvene, which piperidine traps

findings.observation: Several terms are dropped at first use with no gloss, all of them in sections that are already dense. In peptide synthesis: 'E1cb elimination', 'a cyclopentadienyl-type carbanion flanked by two benzene rings', and then a single paragraph containing O-acylisourea, N-acylurea, oxazolone, racemisation, 'uronium or phosphonium reagents such as HBTU or HATU', 'a hindered amine base', and 'a benzotriazolyl ester' - seven unfamiliar species in five sentences, none of them drawn, and none of them assessed anywhere. In enzymes: 'the oxocarbenium-like character that develops at the anomeric carbon' assumes I retained acetal chemistry from the carbohydrate chapter.
findings.learner_impact: I hit 'E1cb' and cannot tell whether it is something I was supposed to learn earlier or something being defined here, so I reread the paragraph twice, get nothing, and skip the rest of the section - including the solid-phase material, which I could have understood.
findings.evidence: nugget-peptide-synthesis expanded: 'an E1cb elimination then expels dibenzofulvene'; 'the anion produced is a cyclopentadienyl-type carbanion flanked by two benzene rings'; 'Current practice therefore couples with uronium or phosphonium reagents such as HBTU or HATU with a hindered amine base, together with an additive that captures the activated acid as a benzotriazolyl ester'. nugget-enzymes-and-catalysis expanded: 'stabilises the oxocarbenium-like character that develops at the anomeric carbon'.
findings.recommended_outcome: Terms that are never assessed and never reused should either be glossed at first use or cut; a struggling reader treats an unexplained term as a signal that the passage is not for them.

location.anchor_text: enzymes, transport proteins, antibodies

findings.observation: Figures are appended after the whole essay rather than placed where the prose needs them, and several are unexplained or repetitive. Every section is one text block followed by all its figures, so by the time I reach the glycine cation, zwitterion, and anion drawings I have already read 5,600 characters about them. Across the chapter 53 molecule blocks are rendered, many repeated verbatim in different sections (glycine appears in five sections, L-alanine in six, all with identical captions). In the protein-structure section, clip-antibody-schematic ('An antibody: four chains, held together by disulfide bridges') is shown although the prose mentions antibodies only inside a three-word list and never explains an antibody's chain structure.
findings.learner_impact: The figures arrive too late to help me while reading and too repetitively to signal what is new, so I scroll past all of them. When I meet a figure whose content the prose never discusses, I assume I missed a paragraph and scroll back, which costs me the thread.
findings.evidence: Compiled reader: every section has exactly one text block at index 0 followed by molecule/image blocks. blk-h0lw26ry, blk-86bzsr13, blk-y7yhgwcw, blk-c6mbzer2, blk-7622gyhq are all 'Glycine: the one achiral standard amino acid', SMILES NCC(=O)O, in five different sections. clip-antibody-schematic sits in nugget-protein-structure-levels whose prose says only 'Proteins built this way are globular and generally soluble - enzymes, transport proteins, antibodies.'
findings.recommended_outcome: Figures need to sit at the point in the reading where they are being discussed, and a figure that introduces content the prose does not cover either needs that content or needs to go.

location.anchor_text: One of the hydrogens on atom 3 (carried implicitly in the drawing)

findings.observation: The bond-change ledger requires me to record two rows involving atom 4, which the question itself describes as 'carried implicitly in the drawing' - an atom that is not shown in the structure I am looking at. Two of the four expected rows (bond_broken 3-4 and bond_formed 2-4) depend on it, and none of the three hints addresses how to work with an atom that is not drawn; hint 3 only tells me to count the atoms in the by-product.
findings.learner_impact: I look for atom 4 in the drawing, cannot find it, and assume the question is broken or that I am reading the wrong structure. Even after I accept that it is a hydrogen I cannot see, I have no confidence about which hydrogen, so I omit both rows and lose half the ledger.
findings.evidence: ch26-peptide-bond-ledger student_config.atom_labels[3]: {'id': '4', 'text': 'One of the hydrogens on atom 3 (carried implicitly in the drawing)'}; answer_key.expected_rows includes {'kind':'bond_broken','atoms':'3-4'} and {'kind':'bond_formed','atoms':'2-4'}.
findings.recommended_outcome: An atom the student must reason about needs to be visible or explicitly locatable in the representation being used; an implicit hydrogen carrying two of four graded rows is not.

location.anchor_text: There are two nitrogens in this molecule. One of them sits next to a carbon that is double-bonded to oxygen; the other does not.

findings.observation: The hint ladder on this core question collapses at level 2. Hint 2 already fully identifies the answer (the nitrogen next to a carbonyl), and hint 3 restates it in different words ('Find the nitrogen with a carbonyl neighbour, then select that nitrogen together with the carbonyl carbon it is bonded to'), so a student who needed one nudge is handed the whole answer and gets no graduated support.
findings.learner_impact: Because I get the answer on the first nudge, I never do the reasoning myself, and I have no idea afterwards whether I could have located a peptide bond unaided in a longer chain.
findings.evidence: ch26-locate-peptide-bond hints[1] and hints[2], quoted above.
findings.recommended_outcome: The intermediate hint on a core-difficulty question should narrow the search without completing it, so the ladder still has a rung left.

location.anchor_text: Glycine has pKa values of 2.35 for its COOH group and 9.78 for its NH3+ group, and an isoelectric point of 6.06.

findings.observation: Glycine's pKa values differ between the reading and the questions. The zwitterion section states 2.34 and 9.60 and uses them in the worked Henderson-Hasselbalch calculation ('7.40 - 9.60 = -2.20'); ch26-match-glycine-ph-species states 2.35 and 9.78 with pI 6.06; and a wrong-answer explanation in ch26-rank-isoelectric-points gives glycine's pI as 'about 6.1'. The pI implied by the reading (5.97) matches none of these.
findings.learner_impact: I wrote 2.34 and 9.60 in my notes and then met 2.35 and 9.78 in a question, so I could not tell whether I had copied the numbers wrong or the numbers themselves vary. I stopped trusting my own notes on pKa values, which is exactly the material where I needed to trust them.
findings.evidence: nugget-zwitterions-and-acid-base-behaviour standard/expanded: 'The alpha-carboxyl group of glycine has a pKa of 2.34 and its alpha-ammonium ion has a pKa of 9.60.' ch26-match-glycine-ph-species prompt_text as quoted. ch26-rank-isoelectric-points wrong_answer_explanations: 'its pI is simply the average of the alpha-carboxyl and alpha-ammonium pKa values, about 6.1'.
findings.recommended_outcome: One set of pKa values for a given compound across prose and assessment, so a student who memorises the reading recognises the numbers when they reappear.

location.anchor_text: predict whether the side-chain carboxyl of glutamic acid (pKa 4.3) or that of aspartic acid (pKa 3.9) should be more acidic before you look at the numbers

findings.observation: This practice check asks me to predict something the same nugget has already told me, two paragraphs earlier and with the same reasoning: 'which is why the side-chain carboxyl of aspartic acid (pKa 3.9), separated from the ammonium group by one CH2, is more acidic than the side-chain carboxyl of glutamic acid (pKa 4.3)'. The prompt even supplies both pKa values while instructing me to answer 'before you look at the numbers'.
findings.learner_impact: The one place in this section where I would have tested myself instead tests whether I can scroll up. I answer it correctly, feel confident, and have practised nothing.
findings.evidence: nugget-zwitterions-and-acid-base-behaviour.practice_check.prompt versus the expanded tier sentence quoted above.
findings.recommended_outcome: A retrieval prompt needs to require something the surrounding text does not already state and answer; this one needs a case the section has not worked.

location.anchor_text: H2, chiral rhodium-phosphine catalyst

findings.observation: This route builder offers five reagents and four intermediates but carries exactly one wrong_answer_explanation, for the methyl-iodide route. The most attractive distractor for a student who has just read that section - 'H2, chiral rhodium-phosphine catalyst', which the prose presents as the way to get a single enantiomer - produces only the generic feedback, which mentions the racemate but never says why the chiral catalyst does not apply to this substrate. The same section's headline trap, the Strecker carbon count ('Getting that carbon count wrong is the single most common error on Strecker problems'), is not assessed by any surfaced question at all; it is exercised only in the practice check, which does not reach the reader.
findings.learner_impact: I reach for the chiral catalyst because the chapter told me it delivers a single enantiomer, get marked wrong, and receive feedback about a different mistake. I leave believing the catalyst is a general fix I applied at the wrong moment, rather than learning what it actually acts on. And the one error the chapter warns me is most common is one I never get to make and be corrected on.
findings.evidence: ch26-amidomalonate-leucine-route student_config.reagents includes r_h2_chiral and r_nabh4; feedback_bundle.wrong_answer_explanations has a single entry, matching the r_alkylate_me route. nugget-amino-acid-synthesis expanded: 'Getting that carbon count wrong is the single most common error on Strecker problems.' No surfaced question covers the Strecker route.
findings.recommended_outcome: The distractors a student is most likely to choose need feedback that names the discriminating idea, and the error the chapter identifies as most common needs a place where the student can make it and be corrected.

strengths: The wrong-answer explanations are consistently better than 'not quite' - almost every one names the discriminating idea and points at the specific atom or pKa that decides it (for example ch26-sort-side-chain-classes on glutamine: 'Putting a nitrogen where the second oxygen would be removes the acidic proton entirely, and the amide nitrogen is not basic enough to accept one either'), and the $missing matchers mean I am also told why an option I left out belonged.

The cysteine R/S passage is the clearest treatment of a confusing point in the chapter: it states the result, states the reason, and then states in bold what did NOT change ('and no atom has moved'), which is exactly the reassurance a shaky student needs at that moment.

The isoelectric-point section does what the synthesis and peptide-synthesis sections do not - it works four separate cases (alanine, aspartic acid, lysine, histidine) by the same explicit procedure, walking the charge down from the fully protonated species each time, so I can see the method rather than only the recipe.

The zwitterion section opens by making a prediction and letting it fail ('Use it to predict physical properties and every prediction fails'), which gave me a reason to care about the answer before the answer arrived.

The hint ladders on most questions genuinely ladder - strategy first, then what to look at, then the deciding rule (ch26-histidine-isoelectric-point and ch26-aspartate-electrophoresis-reasoning are both good examples) - and the generic_incorrect_explanations read like a teacher reteaching rather than a scoring rubric.

The practice_check answers, where they exist, are real explanations rather than restatements; the protein-structure one in particular explains why activity is lost by tying it to a tertiary-structure active site, which is the connection the section's prose only implies.
open_questions: Is the reader supposed to expose the terse and standard tiers at all? If it is, the compiled chapter JSON cannot support it, since only the expanded markdown is present - which would make finding stud-001 a compilation bug rather than an authoring choice.

Are practice_check and the three video_briefs intended to reach the reader surface for topic chapters, or are they only for the teaching-package view? [internal source reference — not in this repo] renders practiceCheck, but the reader chapter renderer has no such block type.

The reader-side questions file (frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/biomolecules-amino-acids-peptides-and-proteins.questions.json) carries only prompts and metadata - no options, hints, or feedback. I assume the full bank is served from the backend when a student actually works the questions; if not, every hint and wrong-answer explanation I reviewed is invisible to the student and my scores for those questions would drop sharply.

ch26-build-l-alanine-fischer uses the config key 'sugar_display_name' with the value 'L-alanine'. If any part of the interface renders the word 'sugar' to the student on an amino acid question, that is an additional confusion I could not verify from the JSON.

ch26-peptide-bond-ledger expects rows involving an implicit hydrogen (stud-019). I could not determine from the package whether the ledger interface lets a student reference an atom that is not rendered; if it does not, that finding is more severe than medium.

personas.summary: The authored accessibility content in this chapter is the strongest I have seen in this pipeline: all 39 assets carry an alt_text plus a long_description that teaches the figure rather than naming it, the comparison pairs (Ala-Gly vs Gly-Ala, the three glycine ionisation states, myoglobin's helices vs GFP's barrel, myoglobin vs haemoglobin) are differentiated in exactly the respects the comparison turns on, all 40 question accessible_descriptions convey the task without the verdict, the prose never depends on figure position or colour, and the deferred video briefs record captions/transcript/no-colour-or-motion-alone as production requirements. What fails is delivery, not authoring. Three barriers are hard: (1) the 40 accessible_descriptions are never rendered on any student surface - only two renderers in the codebase read accessibilityBundle.accessible_description and neither question type appears here, so the chapter's entire non-visual stimulus-equivalence strategy is inert; (2) the two hotspot items give a screen-reader user atom buttons named 'C atom 4' / 'N atom 6' over an image whose alt is 'Structure for this question', with no chemical identification of any atom, making 'click the two atoms joined by the peptide bond' unanswerable except by guessing; (3) the two structure_scaffold items are a blank Ketcher iframe with no text/SMILES response path, which the platform registry itself records as keyboard_complete=False. Below those, the compiler drops every long_description on the way to the reader, so the eight reader image blocks arrive with alt text only and, unlike molecule blocks, no visible 'Described as:' line - the prose fortunately carries the same chemistry, which is what keeps this from being a fourth blocker. The remaining interactive types (curved_arrow, fischer, bond_change_ledger, synthesis_route, comparison_matrix, categorize_groups, matching_pairs, rank_order, structured_reasoning, walkthrough, error_repair) all have genuine keyboard-and-screen-reader response paths with chemically named options, and the curved_arrow site labels in particular are a model of how the hotspot items should have been configured.

location.anchor_text: A dipeptide is drawn as a line structure with ten selectable heavy atoms

findings.observation: Every one of the 40 questions carries an accessibility_bundle.accessible_description, and every one of them is well written - but no student-facing surface renders it. The LMS activity shell's prompt panel renders only question.promptText; a repository-wide search shows accessibilityBundle.accessible_description is consumed by exactly two renderers (MolecularGeometryRenderer, ReactionCoordinateQuestionRenderer) plus the internal QuestionTypeDemoPage, and none of the 40 questions here uses either of those two types. A learner who cannot see the stimulus therefore receives the prompt text and a bare widget with no description of what is shown.
findings.learner_impact: Blind and low-vision learners, and anyone using a screen reader or text-only client, get no stimulus at all for the 26 questions that show structures. For ch26-identify-nonpolar-side-chain they hear four option names with no side-chain information; for ch26-sequencing-plan-repair the dipeptide is announced only as 'Structure for the flawed step'; for ch26-amidomalonate-leucine-route the start and target structures are pictures whose alt text is the entry's short label. The chapter's whole non-visual equivalence plan is written down and then discarded at render time.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] and nothing from `envelope.question.accessibilityBundle`. The authored text that never appears, e.g. ch26-locate-peptide-bond: "A dipeptide is drawn as a line structure with ten selectable heavy atoms — five carbons, two nitrogens and three oxygens — including one methyl branch, two carbon–oxygen double bonds and one hydroxyl. Every atom in the drawing is a clickable region. The task is to select the two directly bonded atoms that the question names." Backend does carry it ([internal source reference — not in this repo]), so the data reaches the client and is dropped there.
findings.recommended_outcome: The non-visual stimulus equivalent that the chapter already contains for all 40 questions needs to actually reach a student on the surfaces the questions are delivered on, for every question type - not only the two types that happen to read the field today. Until it does, the descriptions are metadata, not access.

location.anchor_text: Click that single atom.

findings.observation: Both hotspot items identify atoms only by RDKit index. student_config carries just `molecule_smiles` and `select_count`; there is no regions/sites list. The renderer therefore names each clickable atom `${atom.symbol} atom ${atom.index + 1}` and gives the structure image the alt text 'Structure for this question'. A non-visual learner tabbing the workspace hears 'C atom 1, C atom 2, C atom 3, C atom 4, O atom 5, N atom 6...' with no connectivity, no functional-group identity, and no way to tell the amide nitrogen from the free N-terminal amine - which is precisely the discrimination both questions test. The question type's own manifest promises a non-visual mode this configuration does not supply.

The same chapter shows the fix already exists: the two curved_arrow items on the same concept configure `sites` with labels such as 'The amide nitrogen of the peptide bond', and their atom buttons are announced with those names.

location.anchor_text: A blank drawing canvas is provided, and the task is to draw the product.

findings.observation: Both structure_scaffold items are `{"scaffold":"blank_canvas"}` and are delivered as an embedded Ketcher drawing iframe with no alternative response path - no SMILES entry, no name entry, no assembly-from-fragments mode. The platform's own registry records this honestly.

Both are graded, autogradable questions. The peptide-synthesis concept retains two comparison_matrix items that are fully accessible, so the concept is not lost - but these two specific items are uncompletable, and a learner assigned the whole set is scored on questions they were never able to attempt.

location.anchor_text: Ribbon diagram of green fluorescent protein

findings.observation: Every asset in the topic package carries a substantial `long_description`, and the compiled reader chapter contains zero occurrences of the field - the compiler emits only `alt_text` (and, for molecules, `description`, which is the learning_goal rather than the long description). The eight reader `image` blocks therefore reach the student with alt text alone, and ReaderProviderImage renders that alt text only in the `alt` attribute - unlike StructureCard, which prints a visible 'Described as: ...' line for every molecule. The structural chemistry that makes the six PDB figures teachable - the i to i+4 backbone hydrogen bond in the helix, the strand-to-strand N-H to C=O bond that closes the barrel, the difference between haemoglobin's non-covalent subunit contacts and insulin's covalent bridges, the Glu35/Asp52 pair facing each other across the lysozyme cleft - exists only in the discarded long_descriptions.
findings.learner_impact: For the helix-versus-sheet comparison the chapter is built around, a non-visual learner gets shape words only ('eight coiled helical segments' vs 'eleven flat arrow-shaped strands ... curved round into a closed cylinder') and no statement of what holds either together, so the two figures are distinguishable but the chemical point of the comparison is not carried by the figures at all. The section prose does state the hydrogen-bond patterns, which keeps this from being fatal; the cost is that the figures become decorative for anyone relying on text, and any surface that reuses these assets without the prose (deck, LMS export, PDF) loses the content entirely.
findings.evidence: `grep -c long_description frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/biomolecules-amino-acids-peptides-and-proteins.json` returns 0. Authored but unreachable, pdb-gfp-beta-barrel.long_description: "Eleven of them lie alongside one another, hydrogen bonded between the N-H of one strand and the C=O of its neighbour, and the resulting sheet curves round until its edges meet, forming a closed barrel." Compiled block blk-xfimmx13 content keys are exactly {url, alt_text, caption}. [internal source reference — not in this repo], `{content.caption}`, `{content.attribution}` and nothing else.
findings.recommended_outcome: The longer structural description each figure already has needs to survive compilation and be available at the figure in the reader, in a form a screen reader and a sighted reader can both reach, so the protein figures teach rather than decorate.

location.anchor_text: Structures and diagrams

findings.observation: The reader personalization control 'Structures and diagrams' removes molecule, reaction, reaction_coordinate and image blocks from the chapter entirely rather than collapsing them to their text equivalent. personas.summary: The chapter is figure-rich by count and figure-poor by kind. Sixty-one figure slots are filled from 39 unique assets, but 38 of the 39 are static single structures or whole-protein ribbon renders: there is not one reaction scheme, arrow, cycle, axis, plot, or annotated geometry anywhere in the chapter. That mismatch bites hardest exactly where the prose is doing spatial or temporal work. The alpha-helix (right-handed, 3.6 residues per turn, N-H of i+4 to C=O of i, side chains 100 degrees apart) and the parallel-versus-antiparallel sheet with side chains alternating above and below the plane are carried entirely by sentences; the five images in that section are whole-protein views that cannot resolve a single hydrogen bond. The planar six-atom peptide plate, phi/psi, cis/trans and the Ramachandran result are likewise words-only beside five flat 2D structures. The titration curve is walked through plateau by plateau and never drawn; the charge ladder is stepped +1/0/-1/-2 in prose while the accompanying figures show aspartic acid and lysine as fully neutral free bases, species that exist at no pH. The Edman cycle and the solid-phase cycle appear only as their endpoint reagents, and all three video briefs are deferred, so nothing in the chapter moves or sequences. Placement compounds this: every section is one 5,400-8,700 character prose block followed by a trailing gallery, and the prose never once refers to a figure, so no figure sits with the sentence it illustrates. Against that, several clusters genuinely earn their place - the glycine cation/zwitterion/anion triad with explicit hydrogens, Ala-Gly versus Gly-Ala, Boc- versus Fmoc-glycine, cystine, and the haemoglobin and GFP renders - and legibility hygiene is good: show_hydrogens is used on five small molecules only and never on a large one, and no asset sets annotation_font_scale, so there is no stereo-label burial risk. The recommendation is not more media but different media, plus removal of the repeats that carry stale captions into new sections.

findings.observation: The single most geometry-dependent passage in the chapter is words-only. The five images in this section (myoglobin, GFP, haemoglobin, insulin, antibody schematic) are all whole-molecule views at a scale where no individual hydrogen bond, residue index, strand direction, or side-chain face is resolvable. The assessment repeats the problem: ch26-helix-vs-sheet-matrix asks a six-row comparison of helix versus antiparallel sheet on 'nearly fully extended rather than wound up', 'successive side chains point to opposite faces', and hydrogen-bond locality, with zero structure_smiles and no figure of any kind.
